title: MET tyrosine kinase inhibitors in combination with EGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitors in NSCLC patients with EGFR mutations and acquired MET alterations: a systematic review and meta-analysis
author: Defeng Hu; Yixuan Hu; Shipeng Lei; Dongdong Wu; Yubo Wang
text:
Abstract
Background
Acquired MET alterations is one of the resistance mechanisms to advanced NSCLC patients treated with EGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKIs). Several clinical trials combined MET-TKI (such as capmatinib, tepotinib, savolitinib) with EGFR-TKI to overcome MET alterations resistance. We performed this meta-analysis to determine the efficacy and safety of MET-TKI plus EGFR-TKI combined therapy in NSCLC patients.
Methods
Pubmed, Embase and the Cochrane Library were searched for relevant studies up to August 19, 2024. Data of objective response rate (ORR), disease control rate (DCR), progression-free survival (PFS), median duration of response (mDOR) and adverse events were extracted from the publications and analyzed.
Results
Six studies involving 562 patients were included in this meta-analysis. Our study showed a pooled ORR of 49.2% (95% confidence interval [CI] 0.402–0.582), a pooled DCR of 78.6% (95%CI 0.680–0.893), a mDOR of 6.85 months (95%CI 5.85–7.86), and a mPFS of 5.62 months (95%CI 4.74–6.50) in MET-TKI plus EGFR-TKI combination therapy for NSCLC patients with acquired MET-driven resistance after EGFR-TKI treatment. The pooled efficacy data suggested that combining MET-TKI with a third-generation EGFR-TKI was numerically superior to combining MET-TKI with a first-generation EGFR-TKI in patients who were T790M negative with MET-dependent resistance mechanism (ORR: 56.8% vs. 47.8%, p = 0.15; DCR: 81.6% vs. 75%, p = 0.57; mDOR: 9.08 vs. 7.00 months, p = 0.25; mPFS: 7.45 vs. 4.55 months, p = 0.05). The efficacy data of capmatinib plus EGFR-TKI, savolitinib plus EGFR-TKI and tepotinib plus EGFR-TKI (regardless of generation of EGFR-TKIs) was similar (ORR:47.7% vs. 50.7% vs. 48.8%, p = 0.96; DCR: 71.4% vs. 84.9% vs. 63.3%, p = 0.02; mDOR: NR vs. 8.4 vs. 8.01 months, p = 0.18; mPFS: 5.49 vs. 6.88 vs. 5.48 months, p = 0.56). Capmatinib subgroup seemed to demonstrate lower hepatotoxicity compared with savolitinib and tepotinib subgroups numerically (increased AST level: 12.8% vs. 18.8% vs. 17.4%, p = 0.66; increased ALT level: 14.2% vs. 17.6% vs. 20.1%, p = 0.91). And a lower occurrence rate of ≥ 3 grade TRAEs was observed in the capmatinib subgroup compared to the savolitinib or tepotinib subgroups (30.0% vs. 46.7% vs. 41.2%, p = 0.07).
Conclusion
The findings from this meta-analysis suggest that the combination of MET-TKI and EGFR-TKI represents a promising therapeutic approach for NSCLC patients who have acquired MET alterations following EGFR-TKI treatment. Notably, the combination of MET-TKI and a third-generation EGFR-TKI demonstrated enhanced survival benefits compared to the combination with a first-generation EGFR-TKI. Furthermore, different MET-TKIs based combination therapy did not display significant differences in efficacy, while capmatinib based combination therapy showed better safety profile and lower hepatotoxicity.
Introduction
Non-small-cell lung cancer (NSCLC) accounts for approximately 85% of all lung cancers and is the leading cause of cancer-related death in China [1]. Remarkable improvements in the survival rate of NSCLC patients have been observed with the advent of oncogenic driver mutation discoveries and targeted therapy advancements. The MET pathway reportedly plays a crucial role in regulating vital cellular processes under normal physiological conditions [2]. Nevertheless, MET alterations, including protein overexpression, gene mutation, amplification, and rearrangement, can contribute to the onset and progression of many human cancers, including NSCLC [3, 4]. Alterations of MET often occurred as resistance mechanisms of EGFR-TKI therapy, such as MET amplification which has been reported in 5-26% of NSCLC patients progressed with EGFR-TKI [5–10], while MET protein overexpression ranges from 25-75% [11–13].
Over the last decade, several MET inhibitors (MET-TKIs) have been developed and explored in various stages of clinical trials, either as stand-alone treatments or in combination with other agents [14–20]. MET-TKIs including capmatinib, tepotinib, savolitinib, glumetinib and vebreltinib in NSCLC patients with MET exon 14 skipping mutations have received approval from the FDA or China National Medical Products Administration (NMPA). However, none of these MET-TKIs has been approved worldwide for NSCLC patients who have developed acquired MET-alterations after EGFR-TKI progression. In several clinical trials, the combination of EGFR-TKI and MET-TKI was often selected to combat the acquired MET alterations in NSCLC patients progressed on EGFR-TKIs, showing promising responses and tolerable safety profiles [18–20]. Given the heterogeneity of MET alterations, the therapeutic benefits of this combined treatment can vary among patients with differing gene copy numbers (GCN) of MET amplification or MET protein overexpression levels. Up to now, no study has compared the differences in efficacy and safety of various combinations of EGFR-TKI plus MET-TKI in NSCLC patients with acquired MET alterations. Therefore, to facilitate optimal clinical treatment strategies, we conducted this META-analysis of studies, examining the efficacy and safety of the combined use of EGFR-TKI and MET-TKI in NSCLC patients with acquired MET alterations.
Methods
Search strategy
This meta-analysis study was conducted following the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis (PRISMA) guidelines [21]. An exhaustive literature search in PubMed, Embase, and The Cochrane Library was conducted using the key words “EGFR”, “MET” and “non-small-cell lung cancer”. The last date of the search was August 19, 2024.
Selection criteria
Articles reporting the results of clinical trails with prospective design published in English and meeting the following criteria were included: 1) adult patients diagnosed as locally advanced or metastatic NSCLC with MET alterations after EGFR-TKI treatment; 2)combined treatment with EGFR-TKI and Type Ib MET-TKI; 3) reported outcomes of study including objective response rate (ORR), disease control rate (DCR), progression-free survival (PFS), median duration of response (mDOR) and adverse events graded according to the National Cancer Institute Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse Events (AEs).
Meta-analysis, reviews without available original data, the same studies with different follow-up times and duplicated data, and article with only abstract could be located were excluded.
Data extraction
The following data were recorded from the original literature by two investigators independently: (1) first author; (2) year of publication; (3) number of patients; (4) type of MET alterations; (5) treatment details of EGFR-TKI plus MET-TKI; (6) response/outcome including ORR, DCR, mDOR, mPFS and (7) AEs. The characteristics of the included studies are described in detail in Table 1. In the study combining capmatinib plus gefitinib [19], we utilized the efficacy data from the subgroup with a Gene Copy Number (GCN) ≥ 6 to make the study comparable, since the remaining study all have GCN cut off > 5 ∼ 6.

Quality assessment
According to the Cochrane Handbook for Systematic Reviews of Interventions [22], the assessment of the quality of literature includes the following criteria: random sequence generation, allocation concealment, blinding of participants and personnel, blinding of outcome assessment, incomplete outcome data, selective reporting, and other biases. Based on the information provided in the literature, these criteria can be categorized as “high risk“(red), “low risk“(green) or “unclear risk“(blank).
Statistical analysis
Clinical outcomes and AEs of all enrolled studies were analyzed. We conducted a meta-analysis of single-arm trials using the meta package in R (version 4.4.1) and assessed the quality of the included studies using Review Manager, version 5.4 (RevMan; Cochrane Collaboration). In the included studies, clinical heterogeneity has been preliminarily identified. If I² ≤ 50%, we will choose a fixed-effects model. If I² > 50%, indicating substantial clinical heterogeneity, we will use a random-effects model for the analysis. Alternatively, we may employ subgroup and sensitivity analyses to address and interpret the sources of heterogeneity. The subgroup analysis will be mainly based on drug types. Since all included studies are single-arm clinical trials focusing on ORR, DCR, mPFS, and mDOR as endpoints for efficacy assessment, we conducted a meta-analysis using R. We use ORR, DCR, mPFS, and mDOR to assess the efficacy of the drugs, while adverse events reflect their safety. In these single-arm trials, ORR, DCR, and treatment-related adverse events are evaluated using 95% confidence intervals (CI). In the meta-analysis, a significance level of α = 0.05 is used as the threshold for assessing differences.
Results
Search results and study quality assessment
After extensive screening and selection, 6 studies involving 592 patients were incorporated into our current analysis. Figure 1 illustrates this screening process. Among these six studies, one was a phase II randomized controlled trial (RCT) [20], while the remaining five were prospective non-comparative clinical investigations [19, 23–26]. All the studies included patients with MET alterations after EGFR-TKI treatment, but the inclusion criteria varied and were summarized in Table 1. All included patients had advanced or metastatic NSCLC and had demonstrated progression following EGFR-TKIs treatment. Four of the chosen studies considered patients with either MET amplification or MET protein overexpression [19, 20, 23, 24], while two exclusively enrolled patients with MET amplification [25, 26]. These studies investigated the treatments consisting of capmatinib plus gefitinib [19], capmatinib plus erlotinib [23], tepotinib plus gefitinib [20], tepotinib plus osimertinib [26], savolitinib plus gefitinib [25], and savolitinib plus osimertinib [24] respectively. The assessment of the quality of literature was shown in Fig. 2, which were considered acceptable for the present meta-analysis.
Pooled analysis of antitumor efficacy
The pooled ORR is 49.2% (95%CI 0.402–0.582) across six studies involving 404 NSCLC patients [19, 20, 23–26], where the ORRs are between 31% and 67%. Due to high heterogeneity across these studies (I2 = 69%, p < 0.01), we adopted the random-effects model (Fig. 3A).
In determining the pooled DCR, five studies involving 373 patients were included [19, 23–26], exhibiting a range between 50 and 100%. The pooled DCR was 78.6% (95%CI 0.680–0.893) with high heterogeneity (I2 = 88%, p < 0.01) (Fig. 3B).
As for the pooled mDOR, data from four studies involving 360 patients were analyzed [20, 24–26], demonstrating a range of 5.6–11.0 months. The pooled mDOR was determined to be 6.85 months (95%CI 5.85–7.86) with low heterogeneity (I2 = 46%, p = 0.08) (Fig. 3C).
Finally, examining the pooled mPFS, we incorporated five studies involving 396 patients [19, 20, 24–26], revealing a range of 4 to 11.1 months. The pooled mPFS was 5.62 months (95%CI 4.74–6.50) with high heterogeneity among studies (I2 = 58%, p = 0.02) (Fig. 3D).
Subgroup analysis of antitumor efficacy
In our subgroup analysis, we evaluated the pooled ORR for the combination of MET-TKI plus first-generation EGFR-TKI (gefitinib, erlotinib) and MET-TKI plus third-generation EGFR-TKI (osimertinib) using three studies [19, 20, 25], involving 90 patients, and two studies [24, 26], involving 191 patients, respectively. The pooled ORRs were 47.8% (95%CI 0.375–0.581, I2 = 0) and 56.8% (95%CI 0.499–0.638, I2 = 0) (p = 0.15), while the pooled DCRs were 75.0% (95%CI 0.578–0.879) and 81.6% (95%CI 0.637–0.995, I2 = 92%) (p = 0.57) in the plus first-generation group and plus third-generation subgroups (Fig. 4A and B) respectively. Moreover, the pooled mDORs were 7.00 (95%CI 4.1–9.9) and 9.08 (95%CI 7.11–11.04, I2 = 0) months (p = 0.25), while the pooled mPFSs were 4.55 (95%CI 3.99–5.12, I2 = 38%) and 7.45 (95%CI 4.88–10.02, I2 = 65) months (p = 0.05) in the MET-TKI plus first-generation EGFR-TKI and MET-TKI plus third-generation EGFR-TKI subgroups respectively (Fig. 4C and D).
Regardless of which generation of EGFR-TKI, the subgroup analysis showed the pooled ORRs for capmatinib plus EGFR-TKI, savolitinib plus EGFR-TKI, and tepotinib plus EGFR-TKI were 47.7% (95%CI 0.330–0.625), 50.7% (95%CI 0.350–0.664), and 48.8% (95%CI 0.402–0.574) respectively, but with no statistical difference (p = 0.96) (Fig. 5A). The subgroup analysis detailing the pooled DCRs for capmatinib plus EGFR-TKI, savolitinib plus EGFR-TKI and tepotinib plus EGFR-TKI were 71.4% (95%CI 0.583–0.845), 84.9% (95%CI 0.729–0.970) and 63.3% (95%CI 0.529–0.728) respectively, showing significant difference between 3 subgroups (p = 0.02) (Fig. 5B). In reviewing mDOR, the forest plots of the subgroup analysis for savolitinib plus EGFR-TKI and tepotinib plus EGFR-TKI revealed figures of 8.40 (95%CI 5.64–11.16) and 8.01 (95%CI 6.04–9.98) months respectively, without significant differences (p = 0.18, Fig. 5C). Lastly, the forest plots from the subgroup analysis of pooled mPFS for capmatinib plus EGFR-TKI, savolitinib plus EGFR-TKI, and tepotinib plus EGFR-TKI were 5.49 (95%CI 4.21–6.77), 6.88 (95%CI 4.42–9.34), and 5.48 (95%CI 4.74–6.22) months respectively, demonstrating no significant discrepancies (p = 0.56, Fig. 5D).
Toxicity
In analyzing Adverse Events (AEs), we included all patients across the six studies. This involved a total of 592 NSCLC patients, the majority of whom experienced AEs of grade 1–2. As illustrated in Fig. 6A, the pooled data reported that the most common AEs were nausea (36.7%, 95%CI 0.271–0.463), edema (31.7%, 95%CI 0.258–0.377), diarrhea (31.6%, 95%CI 0.222–0.411), rash (27.1%, 95%CI 0.168–0.374), vomiting (25.7%, 95%CI 0.161–0.353), increased AST (17.3%, 95%CI 0.114–0.231), increased ALT (17.2%, 95%CI 0.113–0.232), and pneumonia (7.3%, 95%CI 0.026–0.120). Because edema and hepatotoxicity are relatively common and shared AEs among various MET-TKIs, in the subgroup analysis, we focused on the occurrence rates of edema and increased ALT/AST level. As depicted in Fig. 6B, the incidence of edema across the capmatinib, savolitinib, and tepotinib subgroups was recorded at 31.0% (95% CI 0.245–0.375), 29.7% (95% CI 0.203–0.391), and 38.1% (95% CI 0.306–0.456) respectively, with no statistical significant differences (p = 0.57, Fig. 6B). The rate of occurrence for increased AST level across the capmatinib, savolitinib, and tepotinib subgroups were 12.8% (95% CI 0.082–0.175), 18.8% (95% CI 0.082–0.295), and 17.4% (95% CI 0.059–0.290) respectively, again showing no significant discrepancies (p = 0.66, Fig. 6C). Additionally, the capmatinib, savolitinib, and tepotinib subgroups demonstrated an increased ALT level occurrence rate of 14.2% (95% CI 0.094–0.191), 17.6% (95% CI 0.081–0.271) and 20.1% (95% CI 0.000-0.408) respectively, without statistical significant differences (p = 0.91, Fig. 6D), while capmatinib subgroup seemed to have lower hepatotoxicity numerically.
We collected data on ≥ 3 grade TRAEs from the included studies. The pooled rate of ≥ 3 grade TRAEs was 41.7% (95%CI 0.330–0.505, Fig. 6A). The rates of ≥ 3 grade TRAEs across the capmatinib, savolitinib, and tepotinib subgroups were 30.0% (95%CI 0.236–0.365), 46.7% (95% CI 0.326–0.608), and 41.2% (95% CI 0.247–0.577) respectively, without statistical significant differences observed (p = 0.07, Fig. 7A), while capmatinib subgroup had a numerical lower rate of ≥ 3 grade TRAEs. These ≥ 3 grade TRAEs included edema (4.2%, 95%CI 0.023–0.062), increased AST levels (3%, 95%CI 0.013–0.047), nausea (2.7%, 95%CI 0.011–0.043), vomiting (2.6%, 95%CI 0.011–0.041), increased ALT levels (2.4%, 95%CI 0.009–0.039), rash (1.8%, 95%CI 0.002–0.034) and diarrhea (1.6%, 95%CI 0.003–0.029) (Fig. 7B).
Sensitivity analysis
We performed a sensitivity analysis by changing the pooling models and found that the results were consistent across different models, indicating good stability of the study findings and that the conclusions of this research are stable and reliable.
Discussion
In this meta-analysis, we assessed the efficacy and safety of the combination therapy of MET-TKI and EGFR-TKI in advanced NSCLC patients. These patients demonstrated an acquired MET-dependent resistance mechanism following EGFR-TKI treatment, as reported in multiple clinical trials. Our study, which includes 592 NSCLC patients from six studies, showed promising effects of the MET-TKI and EGFR-TKI combination therapy. Furthermore, our subgroup analysis indicated that for patients with acquired MET alterations and negative T790M, combining MET-TKI and the third-generation EGFR-TKI had a better result than pairing MET-TKI with the first-generation EGFR-TKI. The efficacy data of capmatinib, savolitinib and tepotinib subgroups didn’t show significant differences. However the rates of ≥ 3 grade TRAEs were lower in patients treated with the combination of capmatinib and EGFR-TKI compared to those treated with either tepotinib or savolitinib combined with EGFR-TKI numerically. This makes capmatinib a preferable option for MET-TKI in combination therapy.
MET alterations plays a crucial role in resistance development following EGFR-TKI treatment, especially in cases of progression on osimertinib [6, 27]. Liu’s study revealed that in NSCLC patients with acquired MET amplification after EGFR-TKI treatment, the ORR was only 18.2%, mPFS 2.9 months, mOS 8.5 months in the chemotherapy treatment group [28]. Another research by Wang showed that 42 NSCLC patients with MET alterations (10 MET 14 skipping mutation, 32 MET amplification) were treated with immunotherapy, the ORR was 30.95% and mPFS was 4.40 months [29]. MET-TKI has been proven to be effective in patients with MET alterations. It has been reported that MET activation is different in patients who have acquired MET alterations and progressed on EGFR-TKI treatment from those who are treatment-naïve [30]. Therefore, the combination of MET-TKI and EGFR-TKI could present a promising therapeutic strategy for patients with acquired MET alterations [31]. As Type Ia MET-TKI, crizotinib also showed efficacy in NSCLC patients with MET alterations. Liu’s real-world study showed that 38 patients with acquired MET amplification received crizotinib combined with EGFR-TKI, the ORR was 48.6%, mPFS 5.0 months and mOS 10.0 months [28]. The case series from west population also indicated that adding crizotinib to EGFR-TKI in NSCLC patients acquiring MET amplification at progression on EGFR-TKI monotherapy is a reasonable approach, with a PFS of 3–19 months [32]. In this meta-analysis, we focused on patients who had acquired MET alterations (MET GCN ≥ 5 or MET: CEP7 ≥ 2 and/or IHC 2+/3+) following EGFR-TKI treatment. Our study showed a pooled ORR of 49.2%, a pooled DCR of 78.6%, a mDOR of 6.85 months, and a mPFS of 5.62 months in this combination therapy (Fig. 3). Although not being a direct comparison, these efficacy data appear to outperform chemotherapy and immunotherapy (ORR ranging from 0 to 18.2%, DCR from 50 to 72.7%, mPFS from 2.5 to 2.9 months) in NSCLC patients with acquired MET alterations from previous research, and seemed comparable to the efficacy of crizotinib combination therapy [28, 29, 33]. However, the data of crizotinib combination therapy primarily originate from real-world studies, whereas our meta-analysis exclusively incorporated registered clinical trials of Type Ib MET-TKIs. Due to differences in study enrollment criteria and evidence levels, direct comparisons between these researches are not feasible. We didn’t carry out further subgroup analysis based on MET amplification or MET overexpression, considering the sample size within each subgroup was too small.
In patients treated with the first or second generation of EGFR-TKIs, the EGFR T790M mutation is the most commonly acquired resistance mechanism [8, 34]. Yang’s study showed that the combination of savolitinib and gefitinib achieved an ORR of only 9% in patients with T790M positive and MET amplification [25]. However, in the TATTON study, the combination of savolitinib and osimertinib was able to reach an ORR of 67% in patients positive for T790M and having MET alterations [24]. Hence, for patients harboring both the T790M mutation and MET alterations as acquired resistance mechanisms, it is undoubtedly beneficial to use MET-TKI in combination with a third-generation EGFR-TKI to combat resistance. However, for patients who are T790M negative and show MET alterations after first-generation EGFR-TKI treatment, it remains unclear whether a combination of MET-TKI with the first-generation EGFR-TKI is sufficient or whether switching to a third-generation EGFR-TKI might yield better results. To answer this question, we conducted a subgroup analysis within our meta-analysis. The pooled efficacy data suggested that combining MET-TKI with a third-generation EGFR-TKI was superior to combining MET-TKI with a first-generation EGFR-TKI in patients who were T790M negative with MET alterations after first-generation EGFR-TKI treatment numerically (ORR: 56.8% vs. 47.8%; DCR: 81.6% vs. 75%; mDOR: 9.08 vs. 7.00 months, mPFS: 7.45 vs. 4.55 months) (Fig. 4). One potential reason for this might be that third-generation EGFR-TKIs, like osimertinib, can irreversibly bind to the EGFR mutation, while first-generation EGFR-TKIs bind reversibly, which can result in a better prognosis for patients treated with third-generation EGFR-TKIs [35, 36]. Therefore, for patients presenting a MET-dependent resistance mechanism, irrespective of their T790M status, we recommend subsequent treatment with a combination of MET-TKI and a third-generation EGFR-TKI.
Different combinations of MET-TKI plus EGFR-TKI have been reported to improve the prognosis of NSCLC patients with acquired MET alterations. However, no study has compared the efficacy and safety of various combinations. Inconsistent inclusion criteria for MET amplification or overexpression across different clinical trials make it challenging to compare the efficacy of different MET-TKI plus EGFR-TKI combinations. Previous studies have noted that patients with a higher GCN for MET amplification respond better to MET-TKI treatments than those with a lower GCN [19, 37]. Clinical trials of capmatinib have suggested that a GCN ≥ 6 might be associated with a satisfactory anti-tumor effect [14, 38]. Therefore, in the clinical trial examining the combination of capmatinib and gefitinib, the subgroup data for patients with a MET GCN ≥ 6 was extracted and used in this meta-analysis. Our findings imply that for NSCLC patients experiencing acquired MET alterations, the effectiveness of various combinations like capmatinib plus EGFR-TKI, savolitinib plus EGFR-TKI, and tepotinib plus EGFR-TKI, portray similar efficiency in terms of ORR, mDOR, and mPFS (Fig. 5). However, we noted that in the capmatinib subgroup, capmatinib was only combined with a first-generation EGFR-TKI, while in the savolitinib and tepotinib subgroups, they were also combined with a third-generation EGFR-TKI, but also third-generation EGFR-TKI. Therefore, the numerically superior efficacy data of the savolitinib group might be attributed to the fact that the majority of the analyzed data was combined with the third-generation EGFR-TKI.
Our results indicated that selective MET-TKIs combining with EGFR-TKI were generally well-tolerated in NSCLC patients. The most commonly occurring AEs were edema, gastrointestinal related AE and rash, most of which were mild. Although the occurrence rate of edema didn’t show significant differences among these three MET-TKI subgroups (31.0% vs. 29.7% vs. 38.1%, p = 0.57), capmatinib seemed to demonstrate lower hepatotoxicity. Specifically, increased AST and ALT AE rates were numerically lower in the capmatinib subgroup than in the savolitinib and tepotinib subgroups (12.8% vs. 18.8% vs. 17.4%, p = 0.66; 14.2% vs. 17.6% vs. 20.1%, p = 0.91) (Fig. 6). This result could also be supported by Chen’s research suggesting that capmatinib showcased a manageable safety profile in patients with mild, moderate, and severe hepatic impairment. Significantly, severe hepatic impairment didn’t have a clinically relevant impact on capmatinib pharmacokinetics, making it a more suitable MET-TKI for MET dysregulation NSCLC patients with hepatic impairment [39]. Moreover, in our subgroup analysis, we noted a lower occurrence rate of ≥ 3 grade TRAEs in the capmatinib subgroup compared to the savolitinib or tepotinib subgroups (30.0% vs. 46.7% vs. 41.2%, p = 0.07). Considering that the combination therapy of MET-TKI plus EGFR-TKI might result in a higher incidence of AE compared to using a single drug, selecting safer drugs for such combinations can improve overall safety. Considering the efficacy and safety results generated from our current meta-analysis, we conclude that combining a third-generation EGFR-TKI with capmatinib might be a favorable treatment option for NSCLC patients with acquired MET dysregulation after EGFR-TKI treatment, irrespective of their T790M status.
Emerging evidence suggests that the integration of MET-targeted therapies into treatment sequences may reshape therapeutic strategies for EGFR-mutated NSCLC. The MARIPOSA study demonstrated promising efficacy of first-line amivantamab (an EGFR-MET bispecific antibody) combined with lazertinib, showing mPFS compared to osimertinib monotherapy (23.7 months vs. 16.6 months, HR 0.70, 95% CI 0.58–0.85) [40]. This combination capitalizes on dual EGFR-MET inhibition to delay resistance, potentially altering the tumor microenvironment and reducing MET-driven escape mechanisms. Similarly, the FLAURA2 trial reported enhanced mPFS with osimertinib plus chemotherapy versus osimertinib alone (25.5 vs. 16.7 months; HR 0.62), suggesting that upfront intensification of therapy may delay acquired resistance [41]. However, these first-line strategies raise critical questions about optimal sequencing. For instance, patients receiving amivantamab-lazertinib or osimertinib-chemotherapy upfront may develop distinct resistance profiles, necessitating biomarker-guided approaches in subsequent lines. Preclinical data indicate that MET amplification remains a key resistance mechanism to EGFR-TKIs [42], supporting the rationale for MET-TKIs like capmatinib or tepotinib in later lines in MET-positive tumors. Moving forward, dynamic molecular profiling and liquid biopsy monitoring will be essential to identify MET-driven clones early and integrate MET-TKIs at optimal timepoints, balancing efficacy against cumulative toxicities from multi-agent regimens.
It’s important to acknowledge several limitations in our current meta-analysis. Firstly, our study included a small number of studies and overall patient numbers which could influence the robustness of our findings. Moreover, due to the limited sample size, subgroup analyses for MET amplification or overexpression, as well as histological subtype analyses (lung adenocarcinoma vs. squamous cell carcinoma), were not performed in this study. Secondly, all of the studies we elected to involve were phase I/II studies, with no Randomized Controlled Trials (RCTs) being included. This circumstance necessitates the conduction of larger-scale phase III studies to further confirm the efficacy and safety profiles of MET-TKIs in combination with EGFR-TKIs for acquirement MET alterations. Thirdly, these six studies involve different patient populations and using various testing methods, such as IHC, FISH and NGS, either as single diagnostic methods or in combination. Additionally, they differ in their inclusion criteria, with some focusing solely on MET amplification, while others include MET receptor overexpression. Furthermore, these studies use different cut-off values. Although all these studies represent patients with acquired MET alterations, the above-mentioned differences could lead to biased results.
Conclusion
The findings from this meta-analysis suggest that the combination of MET-TKI and EGFR-TKI represents a promising therapeutic approach for NSCLC patients who have acquired MET alterations following EGFR-TKI treatment. Third-generation EGFR-TKI is a preferred combination option over first-generation EGFR-TKI. Furthermore, different MET-TKIs based combination therapy did not display significant differences in efficacy, while capmatinib based combination therapy showed better safety profile and lower hepatotoxicity.
